assessment_summary: The statement incorrectly claims that the greedy maximum-degree vertex cover algorithm always produces a minimum vertex cover. This is a known false statement in graph theory. By constructing a simple bipartite graph with degrees balanced such that locally optimal greedy choices (combined with adversarial tie-breaking) exhaust the graph inefficiently, the algorithm will return a vertex cover strictly larger than the optimal minimum vertex cover.
counterexample:
Consider the bipartite graph G=(V,E) where:
V = {1, 2, 3, A, B, C, D}
E = {(A,1), (A,2), (A,3), (B,1), (B,2), (C,2), (C,3), (D,1), (D,3)}

Minimum Vertex Cover:
The set {1, 2, 3} covers all 9 edges, so it is a vertex cover of size 3. (Since the maximum degree in G is 3, any 2 vertices can cover at most 6 edges, so no cover of size 2 exists). The minimum vertex cover size is 3.

Greedy Algorithm Execution (with valid tie-breaking):
1. Initial degrees are: A(3), B(2), C(2), D(2), 1(3), 2(3), 3(3). The max degree is 3. Pick A. (Cover={A})
   Remove (A,1), (A,2), (A,3).
2. Remaining degrees are: B(2), C(2), D(2), 1(2), 2(2), 3(2). The max degree is 2. Pick B. (Cover={A, B})
   Remove (B,1), (B,2).
3. Remaining degrees are: C(2), D(2), 1(1), 2(1), 3(2). The max degree is 2. Pick C. (Cover={A, B, C})
   Remove (C,2), (C,3).
4. Remaining degrees are: D(2), 1(1), 3(1). The max degree is 2. Pick D. (Cover={A, B, C, D})
   Remove (D,1), (D,3).
5. No edges remain.

The greedy algorithm returns the cover {A, B, C, D} which has size 4. Since 4 > 3, it did not return a minimum vertex cover. The statement is false.
